q: An online shop in Nairobi expects traffic to spike on Black Friday and drop afterwards. It wants capacity to grow and shrink automatically with demand. Which cloud benefit is this?
why: Elasticity means resources are added or removed automatically as demand changes, so you are not stuck paying for peak capacity all year.
why_not: Data sovereignty is about where data legally lives; it does not adjust capacity.
Manageability is about how easily resources are deployed and operated, not how they scale.
Predictability is about forecasting cost and performance, not reacting to demand swings.

q: A database server keeps running out of memory, so the team resizes it to a larger VM size with more CPU and RAM. What is this called?
why: Vertical scaling (scaling up) makes one machine bigger. Horizontal scaling adds more machines.
why_not: Geo-replication copies data to another region; it does not add memory.
Horizontal scaling adds more instances rather than enlarging one.
Load balancing spreads traffic across instances; it does not resize a server.

q: A team deploys the same application in two regions so it can keep serving customers even if one entire region has an outage. Which cloud benefit does this design show?
why: Reliability is the ability to recover from failures and keep working, which is what multi-region design provides.
why_not: Capital expenditure is a spending model, not a technical benefit.
Consumption-based pricing is how you are billed, not how resilient the app is.
Elasticity is about matching capacity to demand, not surviving outages.

q: Which cloud benefit describes managing and deploying resources through templates, automation, the portal, or command-line tools instead of manual hardware work?
why: Manageability covers how easily you can deploy, configure, monitor and automate cloud resources.
why_not: Depreciation is an accounting concept for physical assets.
Sovereignty is about legal control over data location.
Latency is how long data takes to travel; it is a performance measure.

q: A provider's service-level agreement promises the service will be available 99.95% of the time. Which cloud benefit does this primarily describe?
why: High availability is about keeping a service accessible, and SLAs put a measurable uptime target on it.
why_not: Elasticity concerns scaling with demand.
Governance concerns rules and compliance, not uptime.
Cost predictability concerns forecasting spend.

q: A finance lead wants to forecast monthly spend and application performance accurately before launching a new service. Which cloud benefit supports this?
why: Predictability is the ability to forecast cost and performance, helped by tools such as cost estimators and autoscaling limits.
why_not: Geo-redundancy copies data across regions for resilience.
Federation links identity systems together; it is not a forecasting benefit.
Fault tolerance keeps systems running despite component failure.

q: A logistics start-up stops buying servers and instead pays a monthly bill for the compute it uses. What shift in spending is this?
why: Buying hardware up front is capital expenditure (CapEx). Paying for services as you use them is operational expenditure (OpEx).
why_not: This reverses the direction: cloud moves spending away from CapEx, not towards it.
Hybrid and private are deployment models, not spending models.
Depreciation applies to owned assets, which the start-up no longer buys.

q: In the consumption-based pricing model, what do you pay for?
options: A fixed annual licence regardless of use
Only the storage you reserve, never compute
The full hardware purchase price up front
Only the resources you actually use
why: Consumption-based pricing is pay-as-you-go: no upfront cost and you are billed for what you consume.
why_not: A fixed licence is not consumption-based because it ignores usage.
Compute is billed too; the model is not limited to storage.
Paying for hardware up front is CapEx, the opposite model.

q: Which statement describes capital expenditure (CapEx)?
options: Costs that stop the moment you stop using a service
Monthly charges that rise and fall with usage
Upfront spending on physical assets that lose value over time
Fees paid only to a cloud provider
why: CapEx is money spent up front on assets such as servers and datacenter equipment, which are depreciated over time.
why_not: Costs that vanish when usage stops are a feature of consumption-based OpEx.
Usage-based monthly charges describe OpEx.
CapEx is not about who you pay; it is about buying long-lived assets up front.

q: Which cloud service type gives the customer the most control over the operating system?
options: None; the provider always controls the OS
why: With IaaS you rent virtual machines and manage the OS, patches and everything above it. PaaS and SaaS hand more of the stack to the provider.
why_not: In SaaS the provider manages nearly everything.
In PaaS the provider manages the OS and runtime.
In IaaS the customer does control the guest OS.

q: Employees use a browser-based email and calendar service. The provider manages the servers, software and updates, and the company only manages its users and data. Which service type is this?
why: SaaS delivers a complete application over the internet and the provider runs the whole stack.
why_not: Private cloud is a deployment model, not a service type.
IaaS would require the company to manage the OS and software.
PaaS is for building and running your own applications.

q: A developer wants to publish a web app without managing servers or operating system patches, while keeping full control of the application code. Which service type fits best?
why: PaaS provides a managed platform for your code, so you focus on the app instead of servers and patching.
why_not: SaaS is a finished application; you would not deploy your own code to it.
On-premises means you manage the hardware and everything above it.
IaaS leaves OS management and patching to you.

q: Under the shared responsibility model, which of these is always the customer's responsibility, whatever the service type?
why: Customers always own their data, accounts and identities, and the devices they use. The provider handles the physical layer.
why_not: Host hypervisor patching is the provider's job.
Cabling is part of the provider's physical infrastructure.
Physical security always belongs to the provider.

q: In an IaaS deployment, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system on a virtual machine?
why: In IaaS the customer manages the guest OS, including updates and patches. The provider manages the physical host and datacenter.
why_not: Responsibility is divided by layer, not split equally.
An internet provider has no role in patching your VM.
The provider only patches the underlying host in IaaS, not your guest OS.

q: Which responsibility always belongs to the cloud provider, in every service type?
why: Physical hosts, networks and datacenters are always the provider's responsibility.
why_not: Data classification is the customer's responsibility.
User permissions are managed by the customer.
Customer devices are always managed by the customer.

q: A hospital keeps patient records in its own datacenter but runs analytics in the public cloud, with the two environments connected. Which cloud model is this?
why: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises or private infrastructure with public cloud services.
why_not: Private cloud alone would not use public cloud analytics.
Community cloud is not one of the models tested here and does not fit this scenario.
Public cloud alone would not keep records in the hospital's own datacenter.

q: Which statement describes a private cloud?
options: Infrastructure used exclusively by a single organization
A cloud where the provider owns no hardware
Services shared openly among many unrelated customers over the internet
Services that run only on mobile devices
why: A private cloud is dedicated to one organization, whether hosted on-premises or by a provider.
why_not: Some entity always owns the hardware.
Shared multi-tenant services over the internet describe a public cloud.
Private cloud has nothing to do with mobile devices.

q: A retailer runs its core systems in its own datacenter but rents public cloud capacity only during seasonal peaks. Which statement describes this approach?
options: It is a private cloud because the retailer owns some hardware
It is a public cloud because rented capacity is involved
It is a hybrid cloud that uses public cloud capacity to handle overflow
It is a SaaS deployment because customers use the shop in a browser
why: Mixing your own datacenter with public cloud capacity, for example to absorb seasonal peaks, is a hybrid cloud.
why_not: Private cloud alone would not use rented public capacity for peaks.
Public cloud alone would mean the retailer's core systems are not in its own datacenter.
SaaS describes a service type, and customers using a browser does not define the deployment model.

q: What is a main benefit of the public cloud model for a small business?
options: The business must buy and house all of its own servers
The hardware is dedicated to only that one business
The business must run its own physical security team
No upfront hardware purchase, and the provider maintains the datacenter
why: In a public cloud the provider owns and maintains the hardware, so small businesses avoid large upfront costs.
why_not: Buying and housing servers is what a private on-premises model requires.
Dedicated hardware for one organisation describes a private cloud.
Physical security of the datacenter is the provider's job in public cloud.

q: What is an Azure region?
options: A single rack of servers inside a datacenter
A geographic area containing one or more datacenters connected by a low-latency network
A billing account that groups subscriptions
why: A region is a set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected through a dedicated regional network.
why_not: A rack is much smaller than a region.
Virtual networks are a networking construct inside a region.
Billing groupings are subscriptions or accounts, not regions.

q: A company needs its application to keep running if a single datacenter in a region fails. What should it use?
why: Availability zones are physically separate locations within a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking.
why_not: Tags label resources for organisation and cost tracking.
Locks stop accidental deletion; they do not provide failover.
Management groups organise subscriptions.

q: Which statement about Azure region pairs is true?
options: Customers create and pay separately for each pairing
Planned platform updates are rolled out to only one region in a pair at a time
Paired regions must be on different continents
All data is copied between paired regions automatically at no cost
why: Region pairs support disaster recovery, and planned updates are sequenced so only one region in a pair is updated at a time.
why_not: Pairings are defined by the platform, not purchased by customers.
Pairs are within the same geography, not across continents.
Replication depends on the service and redundancy option you choose; it is not automatic and free for all data.

q: Which option lists the Azure organisational hierarchy from broadest to narrowest?
options: Management group, resource group, subscription, resource
Subscription, management group, resource, resource group
Resource group, management group, subscription, resource
Management group, subscription, resource group, resource
why: Management groups contain subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups, and resource groups contain resources.
why_not: Subscriptions contain resource groups, so subscription must come before resource group.
Management groups sit above subscriptions, not below.
Resource groups sit inside subscriptions, not above management groups.

q: How many resource groups can a single Azure resource belong to at one time?
options: None; resource groups only hold subscriptions
why: Every resource lives in exactly one resource group, though you can move it to another one.
why_not: Resources cannot be in several resource groups at once.
There is no limit of three.
Resource groups hold resources, not subscriptions.

q: A developer wants to run a small piece of code whenever a file is uploaded, without managing any servers, and pay only when it runs. Which service fits best?
why: Azure Functions is serverless and event-driven: code runs in response to triggers and you pay for execution.
why_not: Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps to users.
VMs need you to manage the OS and run all the time.
AKS orchestrates containers and is heavier than this need.

q: A company is migrating an older application that needs a specific operating system version and full administrative access. Which compute option fits?
why: Virtual machines give you full control of the OS, which suits lift-and-shift of legacy workloads.
why_not: Logic Apps automate workflows; they are not a place to host an app needing OS access.
Functions abstract away the OS, so you cannot control it.
DNS resolves names; it does not run applications.

q: Which service automatically increases or decreases the number of identical virtual machines based on demand?
why: Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage a group of identical VMs and can autoscale them.
why_not: Azure Files provides file shares.
Resource Manager is the deployment layer, not a scaler of VM counts.
Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains but do not autoscale.

q: A team runs dozens of containerised microservices and needs automated deployment, scaling and management of them. Which service is designed for this?
options: Azure Container Instances for a single quick container
why: AKS is a managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating many containers.
why_not: Virtual Desktop delivers Windows desktops.
Container Instances run individual containers quickly but without full orchestration.
Blob Storage stores objects, not containers.

q: A firm wants staff to use a Windows desktop and apps hosted in the cloud from any device, including personal laptops. Which service provides this?
why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtualised desktops and apps accessible from many devices.
why_not: Functions run code, not desktops.
Firewall filters network traffic.
Cosmos DB is a database.

q: What is the main purpose of an Azure virtual network (VNet)?
options: To let Azure resources communicate securely and privately with each other, the internet and on-premises networks
To store backups of virtual machines
why: A VNet is your private network in Azure, giving isolation and controlled connectivity.
why_not: Backups are handled by backup services, not by VNets.
Billing is handled by cost management tools.
Monitoring is done with Azure Monitor and related tools.

q: A bank needs a private, dedicated connection from its office to Azure that does not travel over the public internet. Which service provides this?
options: VPN Gateway over a home broadband link
why: ExpressRoute provides a private connection through a connectivity provider rather than the public internet.
why_not: A VPN gateway connection is encrypted but still travels over the public internet.
Traffic Manager routes users to endpoints using DNS.
DNS translates names to addresses.

q: Two virtual networks in different regions need their resources to communicate using private IP addresses. Which feature connects them?
why: VNet peering links networks so resources talk over private IPs on the Microsoft backbone.
why_not: Zones are about resilience within a region.
Policy enforces rules; it does not link networks.
Tags organise resources; they do not connect networks.

q: A company wants to reach its storage account from a virtual network using a private IP address so traffic stays off the public internet. What should it use?
options: A public IP address on the storage account
why: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address inside your VNet through Azure Private Link.
why_not: A public IP does the opposite of keeping traffic private.
Locks prevent deletion or changes, not network exposure.
Advisor gives recommendations; it does not change connectivity.

q: A media company needs to store large amounts of unstructured data such as images and video. Which Azure storage service suits this?
why: Blob Storage is object storage designed for unstructured data such as images, video and backups.
why_not: Policy is a governance service.
Queue Storage holds messages for asynchronous processing.
A virtual network is not a storage service.

q: A company wants to replace an on-premises file server with cloud file shares that staff can map as network drives. Which service fits?
why: Azure Files provides managed file shares accessible over standard file protocols such as SMB.
why_not: Blob Storage is object storage, not a mappable network drive.
Queue Storage holds messages.
Table Storage stores NoSQL key-value data.

q: Which storage redundancy option protects data against a complete regional outage?
options: None; Azure cannot copy data across regions
why: GRS replicates data to a secondary region far away. LRS stays in one datacenter and ZRS stays within one region.
why_not: LRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter, so a regional outage can affect all of them.
ZRS spreads copies across zones but within one region.
Azure can replicate across regions with geo-redundant options.

q: A company must keep records for many years, rarely reads them, and wants the lowest storage cost even if retrieval takes hours. Which blob access tier fits?
why: The Archive tier has the lowest storage cost but data is offline and must be rehydrated before reading.
why_not: Cool is cheaper than hot but still online; archive is cheaper for long-term rarely read data.
Hot is for frequently accessed data and has the highest storage cost.
Premium targets low latency, not cheapest long-term storage.

q: Which Azure service provides cloud-based identity and access management, including single sign-on for cloud apps?
why: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) manages identities and authentication.
why_not: Blob Storage stores data.
Monitor collects telemetry.
The calculator estimates costs.

q: Which is an example of multifactor authentication?
options: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
A password plus a security question
why: Multifactor authentication combines different kinds of proof, such as something you know (password) and something you have (your phone).
why_not: Two passwords are still the same factor type.
A longer passphrase is still a single factor.
A password and a security question are both things you know, so they are one factor type.

q: An administrator wants to require MFA only when users sign in from unfamiliar locations. Which capability enables this?
why: Conditional Access evaluates signals such as location and device, then enforces if-then policies like requiring MFA.
why_not: Locks prevent accidental changes to resources.
Zones are about resilience.
Reserved instances are a billing discount.

q: A support engineer needs to restart VMs in one resource group but must not change anything else. Which feature grants exactly that access?
why: RBAC assigns roles at a chosen scope, so you can follow least privilege.
why_not: Advisor offers recommendations only.
Locks limit changes for everyone; they do not grant a specific person access.
The calculator estimates costs only.

q: Which set lists the core principles of Zero Trust?
options: Encrypt only data at rest, trust signed-in users, keep no logs
Trust the internal network, allow broad access, react after a breach
Use one strong firewall, trust all devices behind it, review yearly
Verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach
why: Zero Trust assumes no implicit trust: verify every request, limit access, and design as if a breach has already happened.
why_not: Trusting all signed-in users and keeping no logs contradicts Zero Trust.
Trusting the internal network is the old perimeter model Zero Trust replaces.
Relying on a single perimeter firewall is the opposite of layered, verify-everything security.

q: What does the defense-in-depth strategy mean?
options: Protecting data with multiple layers of security such as identity, network, compute and data controls
Using one administrator account with maximum permissions
Storing data only in the deepest storage tier
Relying on a single very strong perimeter firewall
why: Defense in depth uses layers so that if one control fails, others still protect your resources.
why_not: One all-powerful account breaks least privilege and creates a single point of failure.
Storage tiers relate to cost and access frequency, not security layering.
A single perimeter control is exactly what defense in depth avoids.

q: Which service gives a unified view of your security posture across Azure and other environments and recommends how to strengthen it?
why: Defender for Cloud assesses security posture, gives recommendations and helps protect workloads.
why_not: Service Health reports on Azure service incidents and maintenance.
DNS resolves names.
The calculator estimates costs.

q: Which network traffic typically generates a data transfer charge in Azure?
options: Data leaving Azure datacenters to the internet
Data coming into Azure from the internet
why: Inbound data is generally free, while outbound data transfer (egress) is charged beyond free allowances.
why_not: Creating a resource group has no data transfer cost.
Signing in is not billed as data transfer.
Inbound data is generally not charged.

q: Before deploying, a team wants to estimate the monthly cost of the Azure services it plans to use. Which tool should it use?
why: The pricing calculator estimates the cost of Azure services you plan to deploy.
why_not: The TCO calculator compares on-premises costs with Azure, not a service-by-service estimate.
Policy enforces rules.
Service Health reports on incidents.

q: A CFO wants to compare the cost of keeping on-premises servers with moving them to Azure. Which tool helps?
why: The TCO calculator estimates savings from moving on-premises workloads to Azure.
why_not: Cloud Shell is a command-line environment.
Policy governs configuration, not cost comparison.
Advisor gives optimisation advice for existing resources.

q: Which tool lets you analyse spending, set budgets and get alerts as costs approach a limit?
why: Cost Management helps you analyse costs, create budgets and receive alerts.
why_not: Firewall filters network traffic.
Arc extends management to servers outside Azure.
Locks prevent deletion or changes.

q: Finance wants cost reports grouped by department across many resource groups. Which feature helps most?
why: Tags are name-value labels you can apply to resources and then use to group costs.
why_not: Zones provide resilience.
Locks protect resources; they do not group costs.
Role assignments control access, not cost grouping.

q: A company will run the same VMs steadily for the next three years and wants a lower price in exchange for the commitment. What should it consider?
why: Reservations give discounts for committing to resources for one or three years.
why_not: Free tiers are limited and not for long-term production workloads.
Spot VMs are cheap but can be evicted, so they suit interruptible work.
Locks are not a pricing option.

q: A security team wants to make sure resources can only be created in approved regions. Which service enforces this?
why: Azure Policy creates and enforces rules such as allowed locations and reports compliance.
why_not: Cost Management tracks spending.
Arc extends management to outside environments.
Monitor collects telemetry and raises alerts.

q: To stop anyone from accidentally deleting a production database while still allowing changes to it, which lock should be applied?
why: A CanNotDelete lock lets authorised users read and modify a resource but prevents deletion.
why_not: ReadOnly would also block modifications.
Audit is a policy effect, not a lock type.
Deny is a policy effect, not a lock type.

q: A CanNotDelete lock is applied to a resource group. What happens to the resources inside it?
options: Only newly created resources inherit it
They are moved to a new resource group
The lock does not affect them
why: Locks are inherited: a lock at a parent scope applies to the resources within it.
why_not: Existing resources inherit the lock too, not only new ones.
Locks do not move resources.
The lock does apply to child resources.

q: Which service helps an organisation discover, classify and govern data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS sources?
why: Microsoft Purview provides data governance, discovery and compliance tooling.
why_not: Container Instances run containers.
Virtual Network is for connectivity.
DNS resolves names.

q: Where can a compliance officer find audit reports and compliance documentation about Microsoft cloud services?
why: The Service Trust Portal publishes compliance, audit and security documentation.
why_not: The calculator estimates costs.
Advisor gives recommendations about your own resources.
Cloud Shell is a command-line environment.

q: What is the difference between Azure RBAC and Azure Policy?
options: They are the same feature with two names
Policy controls which users sign in; RBAC controls network routing
RBAC controls costs; Policy controls identity
RBAC controls what actions users can perform; Policy controls what resource configurations are allowed
why: RBAC is about who can do what. Policy is about what the resources themselves are allowed to look like.
why_not: They are different features with different purposes.
Sign-in is handled by Entra ID and routing by networking services.
Neither is a cost control tool in this way.

q: An administrator must create the same 50 resources in an identical way every week. Which approach is best?
options: Click through the portal each time
Ask support to do it manually
Script it with Azure CLI or PowerShell
why: Command-line tools are scriptable, so repeated tasks are consistent and automated.
why_not: The portal is great for exploring but slow and error-prone for repeated tasks.
Support is not a deployment tool.
Screenshots do not create resources.

q: Which statement about Azure Cloud Shell is correct?
options: It is a desktop app for Windows only
It is a browser-accessible shell that supports both Bash and PowerShell
why: Cloud Shell gives you an authenticated command line in the browser with Bash or PowerShell.
why_not: It supports PowerShell as well as Bash.
It is a shell, not a report.
Cloud Shell runs in the browser rather than as a Windows-only app.

q: A company has servers in its own datacenter and in another cloud, and wants to manage them from Azure. Which service enables this?
why: Azure Arc extends Azure management to servers, Kubernetes and more running outside Azure.
why_not: Blob Storage stores data.
Advisor recommends improvements for Azure resources.
Functions run code.

q: What is a main benefit of infrastructure as code, such as ARM templates or Bicep?
options: Repeatable, consistent deployments defined in code
It removes the need for subscriptions
why: Infrastructure as code lets you define environments declaratively and deploy them the same way every time.
why_not: It does not change licensing prices by itself.
Resources still cost money.
Subscriptions are still required.

q: Which service is the deployment and management layer that receives requests from the portal, CLI, PowerShell and templates?
why: Azure Resource Manager is the management layer all those tools call to create and manage resources.
why_not: Cosmos DB is a database.
Traffic Manager routes user traffic using DNS.
Key Vault stores secrets and keys.

q: Which service gives personalised recommendations to improve reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence of your Azure resources?
why: Azure Advisor analyses your resources and recommends improvements across those pillars.
why_not: Service Health reports incidents and maintenance affecting your services.
Reservations are a pricing discount option.
Policy enforces rules rather than recommending improvements.

q: Which service tells you about Azure outages or planned maintenance that affect your resources?
why: Service Health provides personalised alerts and guidance when Azure service issues or maintenance affect you.
why_not: Policy enforces rules.
Advisor recommends improvements rather than reporting outages.
Reservations are a pricing option.

q: Which service collects metrics and logs from resources and applications, and can raise alerts?
why: Azure Monitor collects, analyses and acts on telemetry, including alerts.
why_not: Firewall filters traffic.
Storage stores data rather than analysing telemetry.
Lighthouse supports cross-tenant management.
